definition: The person who keeps a project's scope, time, cost, risk, and people all pointed in the same direction, so the team actually ships instead of drifting.
A group of related projects that get managed together on purpose, because coordinating them as one unit delivers more value than running each one in isolation.
Something that keeps being built and improved indefinitely, like an app or service — unlike a project, a product never has a defined end date.
The idea that a project's scope, time, and cost are all linked — push on one (like cutting the deadline) and it usually forces a tradeoff on one of the other two.
Identifying everyone with a real stake in a project's outcome, not just the obvious names like the CEO or the developers, so you know who to plan around before work starts.
A short document written before real work begins that states a project's purpose, goals, and boundaries, so everyone starts from the same shared understanding of what it's for.
A project approach that moves through fixed phases in strict order, like planning then building then testing — it works well when requirements are stable, but struggles once things change late.
A mindset, not one fixed process, that values responding to change and shipping working software over sticking rigidly to an upfront plan or heavy documentation.
A specific Agile framework built around fixed-length sprints, defined roles like the Product Owner, and recurring ceremonies like sprint planning and the daily standup.
The Scrum role responsible for owning and prioritizing the product backlog, deciding what the team should build next based on what matters most.
The Scrum role that helps a team follow the process smoothly, removing blockers and facilitating ceremonies, rather than assigning tasks or approving the actual work.
A short, fixed-length stretch of time, commonly one to four weeks, during which a Scrum team commits to a set chunk of work, then reviews and reflects before starting the next one.
The meeting held before each sprint begins where the team decides what work to commit to, based on priority and how much capacity the team actually has.
The meeting at the end of a sprint where the team shows the work they finished to stakeholders and gathers feedback on it.
A way of managing work that visualizes tasks flowing through columns on a board and limits how much can be in progress at once, so nothing gets overloaded.
The tasks a team is actively working on right now, as opposed to what's still waiting in the backlog or already finished — often shortened to WIP.
A hybrid approach that blends Scrum's structure, like fixed roles and planning, with Kanban's continuous flow, often using a flexible board with a limited amount of work in progress.
Splitting one big project into smaller, more manageable pieces, then breaking each piece down further until it's small enough to estimate and assign to someone with confidence.
A number a team assigns to a task to size its relative effort compared to other tasks — unlike a time estimate, story points don't try to pin down exact hours or days.
A team estimation technique where everyone privately picks a story-point guess, then reveals it at the same time, so no one's guess anchors or sways everyone else's.
The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project — since each task waits on the one before it, if any task on this chain slips, the whole project's timeline slips too.

Extra time deliberately added on top of an estimate to absorb surprises, since estimates are never perfectly accurate — e.g. padding a task you think takes 2 weeks to 2.5 weeks so one bad day doesn't blow the deadline.

Spare room in a schedule that lets it absorb a delay without pushing back the whole project — used almost interchangeably with buffer in everyday PM talk, though formally it refers to how much a specific task can slip before it starts delaying other work.
A chart that tracks how much work is left to do in a sprint or project over time, so the team can see whether they're on pace to finish.
A chart that tracks how much work has already been completed over time, and can also show scope that got added along the way — unlike a burndown chart, which tracks what's left.
How much work a team typically completes in one sprint, used to forecast that same team's future sprints — it's not meant for comparing different teams against each other.
When a project's scope quietly grows beyond what was originally approved, usually in small, easy-to-miss pieces — catching it early keeps it from spiraling.
A short daily meeting where each person shares what they did yesterday, what they'll do today, and what's blocking them — it's for the team, not a status report to a boss.
The full list of work a team could do, ordered by priority, that hasn't been started yet — sprint planning pulls from the top of it.
Regularly reviewing and reordering the backlog, refining vague items and dropping ones that no longer matter, so it's always ready to plan from instead of stale.
Spotting potential problems early and acting on them before they happen, rather than waiting until they've already gone wrong and your options have narrowed.
Taking action to reduce or handle a risk once it's been spotted, instead of just noting it down and hoping it doesn't happen.
Shortcuts or quick fixes taken in the code now that will cost extra effort to clean up later — a real, trackable risk to the whole team's plan, not just an engineering complaint.

An explicit, team-wide agreed checklist, like passing all its tests, that a piece of work has to satisfy before it actually counts as finished — not just one person's private opinion. Commonly shortened to DoD.
A checkpoint that work must pass, like passing its tests, before it's allowed to move forward to the next stage of the project.
A recurring meeting where a team honestly reflects on what to keep doing and what to change, aimed at real improvement, not at assigning blame.

Getting a team to actually follow your direction when you have no formal power over them — you can't hire, fire, or set anyone's pay or promotion, which is normal for a software PM. It works by earning trust through consistency, setting goals people genuinely buy into, and communicating clearly, instead of by giving orders.
A short update, usually for executives, that leads with the headline, like a key risk, instead of drowning the reader in every last detail.
A formal ask to modify a project's scope mid-project, weighed deliberately instead of quietly folded in — skipping this process is exactly how scope creep happens.
An honest review, done after a project ends, of what actually happened, including failures, so the next project can go better.

Short for asynchronous — communicating, like written updates instead of live meetings, without everyone needing to be online at the same moment, which matters a lot for teams spread across time zones.
